stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, a daughter of the house
stops.campa: In the castle the bishops of Toul raised above the meeting of Meuse and Saônelle, a daughter comes to the Bourlémont. She is born of the lady called Fée and of the Seigneur Pierre, and the lady of the house takes her to her breast and is churched for a birth not hers: in every mouth she is the lady's daughter. No clerk of Toul enters her in any roll; the name is real, the page is not there. She is christened Giovanna, Jeanne in the speech of the marches. From this rock the line of the name begins: Giovanna, Giovanni, John, Joan, Jeanne, Juana.

stops.name: Domrémy, the village the family holds
stops.campa: Her father rides the short league down the Meuse to the villages the castle holds, Greux and Domrémy, and the child Giovanna rides before his saddle. The village of a few hearths presses around the little church of Saint-Rémy; the meadows flood silver in spring; the tithe is counted in wool and grain. A Bourlémont will hold these fields for as long as the male line lasts, to the year 1412 exactly, when a girl is born in the house beside this church. Giovanna learns the villagers' names, and the village learns the family's.

stops.name: Domrémy, the Ladies' Tree and the lady Fée
stops.campa: On the Sunday of the Fountains the children of Greux and Domrémy dance under the great beech on Bourlémont land, and the lord's daughter dances with them. The house keeps a romance: that a Seigneur Pierre de Bourlémont met beneath this tree a lady called Fée. The house tells it as an old tale because it is not one: the knight is her father, the lady her mother, the tale her true registry, where no clerk can strike her out. Giovanna hangs garlands, drinks at the healing spring, and watches the magpies quarrel in the high branches, the black-and-white birds that hoard bright things and speak all tongues, whose name she does not yet carry.

stops.name: Brixey-aux-Chanoines, letters from the kinsman canons
stops.campa: Up the Meuse at Brixey, seat of the avoués from whom her house descends, the kinsman canons keep a chapel school, and the family's great churchman, Pierre de Brixey, bishop of Toul, holds the crozier of the diocese. Here Giovanna is given her letters: the psalter, the Latin of the liturgy, a clear hand. The bishop-cousin blesses the child of the castle. What the canons of Brixey pour into her she will pour, in another country and another tongue, into a boy in a merchant's house: Latin first, and under it always the singing.

stops.name: Neufchâteau, the cloth market and the road south
stops.campa: Neufchâteau, the market town under the castle's southern eye, gathers the house's produce: wine, wool and cotton from lands across France. Giovanna walks the cloth stalls with her father and learns the merchandise by hand: weave, weight, dye, the difference a border makes in the price. The road south leaves from this square, toward the Saône, the Rhône, and the family's Provençal branch. In this town, generations on, the last Bourlémont lord will be buried in the church of the Cordeliers, friars of her own son's order, come north to keep the family's graves.

stops.name: Lyon, down the Rhône with the cloth barges
stops.campa: The family goes south the merchants' way: overland to the Saône, then the long water-road down the Rhône with the cloth barges. At Lyon, where the rivers meet, the north changes into the south: the light hardens, the speech turns toward the langue d'oc, the cargo turns from wool to silk and dye. Giovanna, twelve years old, rides the deck among the bales and hears the boatmen's songs change dialect league by league. She is traveling the road her cloth will travel all her life, the road her bridegroom will one day ride to find her.

stops.name: The Bourlémont finca near Tarascon, the singing halls
stops.campa: The Bourlémont of Provence keep a finca in the Rhône plain near Tarascon: vines, olives, warehouses of cloth, and halls that are never silent. Music, song and the love-poetry of the troubadours fill every room of the family's Provençal estates; jongleurs winter here; the gaya ciencia is the house's second liturgy. Giovanna grows between the two seats: winters under the northern castle, summers in the singing south, and the south wins. Here she learns the canso and the alba, the viol and the rose, and the exquisite doctrine that suffering in love is an ecstasy.

stops.name: Tarascon, Sainte-Marthe and the rule of the rose
stops.campa: In Tarascon, under the collegiate church where Martha sleeps, the hostess of the Lord, who tamed the Tarasque with holy water and her girdle, Pica keeps the feast of the saint of the house. In the courts of Provence she learns the other rule too: Andreas Capellanus' code of love, and the discipline of the rose: what is spoken beneath it stays beneath it. A secret carried well, Pierre teaches, is a form of fidelity. She will need the doctrine: her whole life to come is a thing spoken sub rosa, under the roof of another name.

stops.name: Beaucaire, the fair where the merchant finds her
stops.campa: Across the Rhône from Tarascon, Beaucaire holds its fair, and the cloth road of the world runs through it. Among the Italian merchants comes Pietro di Bernardone of Assisi, buyer of fine French cloth, ambitious, Francophile, quick-handed. At the Bourlémont booths he meets the lord's daughter who knows weave, weight and dye better than his own factors, and who answers his Italian in three languages. The tradition of Provence keeps it plainly: the fairs of Beaucaire are where the merchant of Assisi found her. He returns season after season, and not only for the cloth.

stops.name: Saint-Gilles, the pilgrimage toward the land of the prophets
stops.campa: Pica walks the great pilgrimage of the south to the tomb of Saint Giles, third road of Christendom after Jerusalem and Rome, whose port ships crusaders and cloth alike toward the Holy Land. She goes as Pierre's catechism taught her: pilgrimage is the remedy of impossible love. She loves the saint himself, the hermit who drank the red hind's milk and took the arrow in his own flesh to shield her; she will teach him to her son. At the abbey door she watches the sails standing out for Outremer, and lays down a sentence for later: you will travel beneath the cross to the land of the prophets.

stops.name: The finca, Pierre returns from Ganja with the Persian poems
stops.campa: Her cousin Pierre comes home to Provence from the Caucasus, where he traveled as a boy with his father on a mission of trade and diplomacy. At the court of Ganja the poet Nizami took a liking to the young Frank and told him the Shahnameh: Rostam and Sohrab, Bijan's cipher in the pit, Zal serenading Rudaba on her tower, the Azhdaha dragons whose skin-cloaks cure the wounds of the heart. Pierre gives his cousin the poems in Persian, the stories of the court, and the beautiful suffering in Nizami's voice. And he gives her a name: Pica, the magpie.

stops.name: The finca, the five sufferings of love
stops.campa: Pierre sings for Pica, filling the halls of the finca with the philosophy he learned at Ganja: the Khamsa's five sufferings of love, each with its remedy. Unreturned love: therefore profess, for shyness is a sin. Impossible love, across seas or centuries: therefore go on pilgrimage. Forbidden love, Layla and Majnun's: therefore fast. Impotent love, when power fails: therefore give alms. And the fifth wound, the open heart, when God returns our love and the loveliest tragedy begins: therefore pray. Each time he says 'and so we suffer,' he smiles only for Pica. He is ten, her cousin, and she is promised: every suffering he names is already his.
